ns2:section.sectionText: Language is sketchy in its conveyance of thought, relying on listeners to fill in much of the intended meaning through inference. For example, if I say “Hand me the book”, a listener can often infer even in a room full of books which one I mean. Such inferences can be based on the physical setting (e.g., what objects are present, what objects are within your reach and not mine), knowledge about the situation and the speaker (what objects are relevant to the speaker’s goals), and on the preceding discourse (has the speaker already mentioned or implied a particular book). Our tendency to enrich sentences with these and other inferences has been documented in classic studies of memory for sentences within psychology, discourse comprehension in psycholinguistics, and in the field of linguistic pragmatics. Young children make some of these inferences, but struggle to draw other inferences in time to guide language processing. In this course we will read and discuss this literature, exploring what kinds of inferences listeners can make, and theoretical accounts of these inferences within psychology and linguistics. The seminar will include a focus on the development of pragmatic inference-making, asking to what extent the sketchiness of linguistic expression poses challenges for early language learning, versus under what circumstances young learners can make the inferences to figure out what we mean.
